Double gene knockout supercharges CAR-T in mice

ScienceNow! short on a peer-reviewed Nature Version of Record.

Title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs
Authors: Liqun Zhou, Paul A. Renauer, Kaiyuan Tang, Shanshan Li, Zhicheng Luo, Yanzhi Feng, Shawn H. Lin, Feifei Zhang, Daniel Park, Shao-Yu Fang, Grace Vest, Zhihan Zhao, William Dorst, Luojia Yang, Chuanpeng Dong, Xingxin Pan, Lars Klemm, S. Stephen Yi, Nidhi Sahni, Lei Peng, Markus Müschen, Xiaoyu Zhou, Sidi Chen (23 authors)
Journal: Nature (published online 2026-11-04; Article Published 04 November 2026)
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10956-z

CAR-T cell therapy can wipe out some blood cancers, but T cells carry built-in molecular brakes that blunt the attack, especially against solid tumours where many designs still fail.

Zhou, Renauer, Tang, Chen, and colleagues ran a high-throughput in vivo double-knockout CRISPR screen in CAR-T cells, deleting gene pairs together to find combinations that work better than knocking out either gene alone.

The top hit was NR4A1 plus SOCS3. Those double-knockout CAR-T cells showed higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity on transcriptome and functional assays. In several mouse tumour models they drove strong antitumour effects and long-term tumour control, without clear safety red flags in the tests reported. The pair also outperformed several published single-gene and dual-gene engineering benchmarks in head-to-head comparisons.

Limitation: this is preclinical mouse work; a human trial of NR4A1–SOCS3 double-knockout CAR-T cells has not been reported here.

Nature, 2026.

AI hunch, not proven: If NR4A1–SOCS3 double knockout keeps working safely in people, CAR-T designs might routinely cut two intracellular brakes at once — but this paper only tested mice. What do you think?
